title: The other great languages
hookLine: your name in your grandmother's mouth and your teacher's: dhamma and dharma are like that
tomorrow: what happens when every piece of the chant is strung together?

cards: Your name sounds one way in your grandmother's mouth and another in a substitute teacher's. Nobody thinks there are two of you. Buddhist words travel like that.
A book says dharma; a chant says dhamma. A poster says nirvana; a sutta says nibbana. So which spelling is right?
Both. They're the same word in two old languages, Sanskrit and Pali, and once you hear the pattern, you can hear it in your own mouth.

teach.b: Put them side by side. Sanskrit dharma, Pali dhamma. Nirvana, nibbana.
Karma, kamma. Sutra, sutta. Maitri, metta.
Where Sanskrit stacks two different sounds together, Pali often smooths them into one doubled sound: the r drops out, the m doubles. Two spellings, one word.
Then the words kept traveling, and in some languages they weren't respelled at all; they were translated.
In Tibetan, the dharma is chö and the Buddha is sangye. In Chinese, the dharma is fa and the Buddha is fo. Vietnamese says Phap and Phat.
And sometimes a sound rides along almost whole.
The namo at the start of the homage, homage to him, turns up in a Vietnamese temple as nam mo, before the name of a Buddha. Same bow, a different mouth.
None of this makes one spelling the real one. Theravada chanting keeps the Pali; Sanskrit forms fill Mahayana books. Tibetan and Chinese and Vietnamese speakers say it in their own.
It's a little like what the Buddha told his monks at the start of this block: learn it in your own dialect.

how: Theravada temples chant in Pali; Tibetan, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhists chant in their own languages or in old sound-forms of Sanskrit names, and English books mix Pali and Sanskrit spellings.

games.q: what does “the other great languages” mean?
o: the modern languages that replaced Pali in temples
the secret languages monks use only among themselves
the Sanskrit, Tibetan and Chinese forms of Buddhist words

games.q: Sanskrit and Pali — tap the pairs.

s: nirvana and nibbana are two different ideas
the same word in two languages: Sanskrit nirvana, Pali nibbana.
where Sanskrit stacks two sounds, Pali often doubles one: dharma, dhamma
the r drops out and the m doubles; nirvana, nibbana works the same way.
Tibetan and Chinese simply copied the Sanskrit sounds
many words were translated: dharma is chö in Tibetan and fa in Chinese.

games.q: a classmate's essay says 'dharma' and the teacher marks it wrong, because the reading spelled it 'dhamma'. what's the fair note?
o: dhamma is correct: Pali is what the Buddha spoke.
both are right: Sanskrit dharma, Pali dhamma, one word.
dharma is correct; dhamma is a later misspelling.
games.why: two spellings, one word. Theravada chanting keeps the Pali, Mahayana books use the Sanskrit; neither is the 'real' one.

practice: Say each pair out loud, slowly: dharma, dhamma; nirvana, nibbana; karma, kamma. Feel where each one lives: the r rolling behind the teeth, the doubled m pressing the lips.
Then let the sounds go and sit with the one meaning under both.

wordCard.voice: The other great languages: Sanskrit beside Pali, and Tibetan, Chinese and Vietnamese after them. One teaching, many mouths.

orig.note: Sanskrit dharma and Pali dhamma in Devanagari letters: the same word, with the r smoothed into a doubled m.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: two spellings, one word, and more mouths than that. Twenty-seven of twenty-nine.
